The firm delivered net income of $15.3 billion, EPS of $5.57, and an ROTC of 20%.
These results included $658 million net investment securities losses and corporate.
Revenue of $50.9 billion was up 8% year-on-year.

SBCB.

volume and revenue-related expense, as well as firm office hiring and wage inflation.

reserve build of $539 million.

13.9%, down 30 basis points versus the prior quarter, as net income was more than
offset by OCI losses, higher RWA, and capital distributions.
You'll note that we've updated the categories on the RWA walk to make it a bit more useful.
This quarter's standardized RWA increase of about $52 billion is predominantly driven
by an increase in lending across banking, markets, and AWM, as well as the impact of
higher energy prices and increased market volatility.
Now moving to our businesses, CCP reported net income of $5.7 billion.
Revenue of $21.2 billion was up 9% year-on-year, predominantly driven by higher balances and
yield and card, asset management fees, deposit balances, and auto lease income.
A few points to highlight, debit and credit spend grew 10% year-on-year, with continued
momentum across spending categories, including gas and travel, supported by consumer net.
Deposit growth of 4% year-on-year was stronger this quarter, as we continued to grow our
customer base across consumer and business banking, and we retained our number one
position in retail deposit share based on FDIC data.
Client investment assets crossed $1.4 trillion, up 15% year-on-year, driven by market performance
and strong flows.
Next, the CIB reported net income of $8.2 billion.
Revenue of $22.7 billion was up 14% year-on-year on strong performance across the businesses.
IB fees were up 14% year-on-year, reflecting strong performance across products, notably
an advisory.
While our outlook remains constructive, supported by ongoing client engagement, evolving market
conditions have recently slowed activity a bit, so we'll have to see how the quarter
develops.
In markets, fixed income was down 4% year-on-year, with lower revenues in commodities, rates,
and credit, largely offset by higher client flows and currencies in emerging markets.
Equities was up 49% year-on-year, with continued on performance across the franchise,
notably in prime and derivatives.
Turning to asset and wealth management, AWM reported net income of $1.8 billion, with
pre-tax margin of 36%.
Revenue of $6.9 billion was up 14% year-on-year, predominantly driven by growth and management
fees on higher average market levels and strong net inflows, as well as higher loan
balances.
Long-term net inflows were $51 billion, largely driven by continued strength and
fixed income.
AUM of $5.2 trillion was up 13% year-on-year, and client assets of $7.9 trillion were up
15% year-on-year, driven by continued net inflows and higher market levels.
Finally, corporate reported a net loss of $455 million, which included the net investment
securities loss, as mentioned earlier, on revenue of $93 million.

fourth quarter.

quarter.

On expense, we expect the fourth quarter to be about $27.5 billion, with the implied
full year increase reflecting higher volume and revenue-related expense driven by
continued elevated activity levels.

Our first question comes from Ibrahim Bunawalov with Bank of America.
Your line is open.
Hey, good morning.
I guess maybe one question, there's been a lot of discussion around all things AI over
the last couple of months.
Maybe if there are two things that you can address specifically, one, when we think
about the disruption risk to agent-tech AI, I know you've talked about in the past,
maybe just frame that given your visibility into the technology, how you think about
that and also the challenge of implementing agent-tech AI inside a bank given the
emergence of all the rogue agents and does that make it harder for a bank to actually
deploy agent-tech AI as we think about just competitive challenges.
I'll start and you want to jump in?
Yeah, okay.
So on the disruption point, a couple things.
There's obviously been a lot of focus on smart cash solution, which I think is a
small piece of the overall story, but that is live now actually as of the last couple
of weeks, very, very early days and it remains kind of a targeted pilot type thing, but
it is interesting to learn some things about what clients care about and sort of see
how it works to kind of sell a product like this in the field.
So I mean, we're going to come on that in the future, early days, interesting
so far.
I think the bigger picture here is around, you know, there have been a couple of releases
of personal agents this quarter, which have really gotten a bunch of attention in the
market and saw a little bit of a response in, you know, bank stocks around those
releases.
And I guess the way we think about that from our perspective is that on the one
hand, it's nothing new and that, but that doesn't mean that we're complacent
about it.
If you think about what is the nature of the competition that comes from these
agents, it's really the intersection of two things that we've been talking about
for a long time.
One is yield seeking flows.
So obviously we deal today and have dealt with all the various race cycles with a
lot of competition from yield seeking flows and our strategy remains focusing on primary
bank share, not chasing every dollar of yield seeking money.
So that doesn't mean that competitive pressure isn't real.
It just means it's not really new.
The other piece is, you know, competition from FinTech for innovating and providing
great customer experiences.
And we've also been talking about that for a long time and the criticality of
ensuring that we have parity with them and that we're leaning in enough to make
sure that we're giving people the experience.
And so in that sense, the kind of agentic personal agents, whatever stuff, it's
just the intersection of those two things.
That doesn't mean we're complacent develops and what we ourselves offer.
You know, when you take a really big step back from a competitive position, I think
we really like our hand and no small part because of the sort of multiple
decades of investment and the branch network, the value proposition and not
least trust.
I would say internally we use agents to do good things here and we're going
to continue to do that and we do, we'll use it for customers, but our
focus always be do a great job for customers.
And so we're not against agents or for agents, something like that.
There are tools, you use them for customers.
There is a defensive side, which is you've got to make sure our customers
aren't hurt by it.
And so that is of concern, but that's I think of that as an AI
agenda concern, which is heightened because, you know, you don't want rogue
agents and there could be thousands of them.
And so we've always been literally on the side of the client.
If people are using them, they should understand the risk.
There's a liability transfer.
They should understand the liability transfer.
If that is being misused, they should understand being misused.
So, you know, we have to make sure we protect our customer in the
right kind of way.
So we will build, we're building tools to do that too.
In the meantime, we're not going to allow just any agent to come, you
know, outside agent to come in inside the company because it's just too
risky for clients and for Jake and Morgan.
That's good color.
And just separately, I think as we assess the risk of interest rates, maybe
moving even higher than what we saw in the third quarter, maybe your latest
thoughts around how you assess the resiliency of the economy to handle
maybe a 6% rate on tenure and just the fed hiking a few times.
Do you think the risk of a market event or just stress on the economy
is meaningful as we, as we kind of discount that?
I think you have to, we always prepare for all different events,
you know, and that's not the same as predicting them because we want to be
a strong company, helping our clients, our communities, countries around the
world, the sick or thin.
So of course things like that can happen.
I would never take it off the table and they can happen for good reason,
which is a lot of demand for capital, a lot of productivity and things are
fine, you can have a bad reason, you know, in thinking inflation around
the world, they can happen not because it's in the United States,
you have, because what happens overseas.
So not predicting it.
You know, I've always thought there's a higher chance of other people.
I still kind of think that, but there's not a prediction that's just a,
because that is cautious preparation.
Thank you.
Thank you.

NII and expenses in the sense that, you know, despite Jamie's comments,

our preliminary read on expenses suggested that the market's consensus

the macro environment, it's also about how dynamic the investment
